Hi,
I'm interested in working on formalizing the word RAM model (typically used in analyzing time complexities of algorithms). As far as I know, there hasn't been work on this topic, and existing theorems on algorithm time complexities rely on the algorithm specifically advance the TimeM monad under the cost model.
While generating the code isn't the difficult part at this point, even after I manually review the code, it would still consume reviewer attention if I were to pull request it, so I'd like to know what are my options.
There has been some progress on this already. But not in CSLib.

One basic challenge that I believe is unaddressed is actually a missing part of the textbook defintion of RAM models. Normally one assumes that one can store memory addresses in memory cells. This is only true if the address type and the type of data in cells match. Word RAM technically allows O(w) many addressing bits without specifying constants.
The only constant that works from an addressing perspective is 1. Nevertheless a lot of algorithms assume some leeway in how many cells are available.
I see. Where can I find the existing progress?
In my local clones of my library. This is why I am not being overly specific but just highlighting some issues you will encounter

If you want a neat defintion for all RAM models, you will encounter this addressing issue even more acutely. You will have models like Integer and Real RAM where the cells can clearly store values that are not valid addresses. There the solution is to have a cell type that has an explicitly constructor for “pointers”. That’s essentially what I am implementing for word ram as well (pending other things).

Do you have any plan for how to express algorithms in the model yet (e.g. to prove theorems of the form "there exists an algorithm X that run in time O(T(n)) to solve problem Y")? At the moment I can only think of

  • writing the algorithm directly in the low-level representation
  • make a compiler from a (restricted subset of) Lean to the low-level representation
By reductions from higher level query models.
The idea is as long as I can express basic high level operations in RAM, I can write algorithms in the high level operations.
It’s easier to implement a single reduction to RAM from some model A and write 100 algorithms in model A, than write those 100 algorithms in RAM.
I suppose your fork is either https://github.com/Shreyas4991/cslib or https://github.com/Shreyas4991/Algolean? Unfortunately I can't find what you're referring to.
It’s in a local copy as I said. There are several design options to explore here. There are also conundrums about space complexity when you have distinct pointer types.

Looks like @Christian Reitwiessner also has an attempted implementation in https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/issues/611 . Unfortunately it seems to be going slowly (and writing more code is _not_ the solution).

Hi @user202729 ! Unfortunately it looks like formalizing space complexity simply does require a lot of code. But we are making good progress and of course we also need a formalization of RAMs. Which models are used later on to build the higher level proofs does not matter once we establish equivalence.
It would be great to have a generic definition that includes all types of RAMs (maybe even includes the URM type hat already exists in CSLib).

@Christian Reitwiessner Do you think any help may be useful? Probably not with coding (LLM generates code too quickly anyway), but maybe with reviewing and reorganizing and improving the quality of the code)
Oh yes, certainly! Reviews are currently the bottleneck.

@user202729 : I actually don’t mind a PR to my library if you have ideas. Even if you use an LLM to help write code it can be considered a design experiment. If merged, then at some later point they can be upstreamed. I am currently trying to decide which variant of register machines is best to implement and where the cell probe model fits into the model hierarchy (so that I can take cell probe lower bounds and translate them to RAM easily).

@Christian Reitwiessner and @user202729 : here's one draft of word RAM, I am grateful for any feedback and comments. It is a bit too raw to work with directly in my opinion. But it captures one of the basic model variants.

EDIT : I think I found a way to block pure computations from doing anything meaningful. The idea is to use an abstract register type for registers, which cannot be read from without the model.

Update

Here's a second version of the RAM model that is stricter. It only allows finitely many registers and you can't access the contents of the memory directly. It necessitated some design changes in the model side of my query combinator framework because the cost accounting part (for space complexity) got stranger : https://github.com/Shreyas4991/Algolean/pull/90

In a sense the concerns about Free monads allowing free "pure" computations disappears because you no longer have access to the things you are computing with in a pure computation.

pure computation

I think the usual way is to define a programming language for the model and implement an interpreter for it. Which is, if I understood correctly, what the Boole language thing is supposed to do. Downside is you need to implement an interpreter.

Regarding using Lean's statement, I'd imagine using Lean's metaprogramming ability to compile a subset of Lean to said programming language, together with a proof that the compiler is correct, in the sense of ∀ program input, run(compile(program), input) = interpret(program, input))

I will shortly make a separate thread for my updated proposal. Now I have a deeply embedded DSL with the same query model. Funnily enough, it still stays within Prog, but you can't do anything with pure anymore. It's still great to have it in Prog, because of the possibility of using reductions from higher level models.
Here's the thread : #CSLib > WordRAM design proposal for CSLib @ 💬
